new_entities.name: Cognitive rehabilitation after concussion
new_entities.description: Structured cognitive rehabilitation used after concussion or mild traumatic brain injury.

new_entities.name: Cognitive outcomes
new_entities.description: Measured cognitive symptoms or performance outcomes after injury.

edges.effect_quant: The cognitive-and-psychological intervention review found no clear pooled reduction in post-concussion symptoms at 3 to 6 months, although some trials reported better functional outcomes or prevention of persistent syndrome in higher-risk subgroups.
edges.population: adults or military personnel with concussion or mild traumatic brain injury and persistent cognitive complaints
edges.mechanism: Cognitive rehabilitation may improve attention, compensatory strategy use, and task performance through structured practice and psychoeducation. But concussion symptoms often reflect a blend of cognitive, psychological, vestibular, and sleep-related factors, so purely cognitive rehabilitation does not reliably move every outcome in every population.
edges.summary: The best overall reading is mixed. Systematic review evidence finds limited consistent symptom reduction, yet selected trials show benefit in high-risk or structured rehabilitation settings, especially when cognitive work is embedded in a broader multidimensional program.
edges.caveats: The evidence base mixes very different populations, from civilian mild TBI to military service members with chronic symptoms, and the interventions themselves range from therapist-led training to integrated CBT-like programs. That heterogeneity makes it hard to claim a single robust cognitive-rehab effect on concussion recovery.
